utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow you in a language that I can understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman I'm here with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. Any preliminaries. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do have. I need to bring Your Honour up to date regarding the treasury department issue and put some additional information on the record in that regard. Based upon information from the U.S. Embassy last week I called David Mills at the U.S. Treasury and I was advised that I would be issued a licence within 24 to 48 hours of receipt of a letter from me requesting one. That letter was sent, it would have arrived in Washington early on Thursday afternoon. No licence has yet been issued and I have this morning sent another fax to treasury in that regard. I also want to place on the record a short note which I sent to Mr. Larry Johnson, the chef de cabinet of -- the President of our Tribunal. Having had some time to study the 19 June letter to the President from our Richard Newcombe, two things have caught my attention. First of all the CFR requires the issuance of a licence. I was instructed to contact David Mills by telephone to expedite the issuance of a licence. I was advised to submit a letter by fax and that a licence would be issued in 24 to 48 hours. I have yet to receive a licence. Do I not think the Newcombe letter is a licence. It is simply a conditional authorisation. It requires submission by U.S. lawyers of unspecified information by 29 June 2003. What about U.S. lawyers who undertake representations after that date? Also and maybe of greatest concern is this line from the letter: "All such payments must come from sources not currently within the United States or within the possession or control of a U.S. person." I'm not sure what this means. To a very large extent I believe the funds I have been paid here have come in part from contributions by the U.S. through the UN or directly to ICTY. Finally, contrary to representations apparently made to President Meron, there is no language in the letter that would make its authorisation retroactive if to the beginning of my representation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Finally, contrary to representations apparently made to President Meron, there is no language in the letter that would make its authorisation retroactive to the beginning of my representation of Mr. Brdjanin or the beginning of services provided by other U.S. lawyers at the Tribunal. I believe these matters must be cleared up quickly. And I just wanted to make that a matter of record and advise the Trial Chamber that at least in my view, this matter has not yet been fully resolved. And I might say, Your Honour, that if I were asked to provide legal advice to someone in the position I find myself in right now, I, being conservative would advise them that they are not yet on firm ground with regard to this issue. The second thing I want to bring up this morning is this: Mr. Cunningham and I are facing an extraordinarily difficult situation with regard to the current scheduling and the upcoming witnesses. I have been frankly, Your Honour, working beyond what I should have to be prepared for today and in some ways preparing for today's witness is easy compared to what we have to do next week. I'm quite exhausted. I've taken one day off in the last month, which is much less than I should have done. Your advice when I first returned that I need to be careful with my health or I'll pay is good advice. I'm simply unable to do that on the schedule that we are pursuing right now, Your Honour. Especially considering the magnitude of the witnesses upcoming in this case. I think I can make it through this week. Mr. Cunningham is also exhausted. He mentioned to me last night that the work load we have right now is a work load that requires five lawyers, not two. We are trying to train a completely new staff. We have a new case manager, legal assistant. We have a couple of new interns trying to learn how to assist us. We need time. And what I'm asking is this: Bearing in mind that if we had been on the kind of schedule that we pursued throughout the course of this trial so far, we would be at the point right now where we would probably have about a week off, and that's what I'm asking you to let us have next week is a week off. With that week, I think Mr. Cunningham and I can prepare to finish up the rest of this case but I assure you that if we do not have that time, we are not going to be able to conduct proper cross-examinations of the expert witnesses that are coming from the Prosecution. The material, just the material that we have to deal with, is voluminous and huge and difficult. Now, I understand, because we have discussed it, that there is a problem with regard to timing in this case and when we will get to the end of it, at the time we need to get to it. All I can do, Your Honour, is assure you that taking a week next week to give us a chance to prepare properly will not affect the end of this case. I suggest that that bridge can be crossed when we come to it. Whether it involves -- whatever it involves, I think we can get there and I can assure you that we will get there because to some extent I will control that process, with regard to the scheduling of witnesses and things of that nature. That would require adding at least another week to the Prosecution's time to give us that preparation time next week but I just feel that it's absolutely crucial for me to be able to give any kind of adequate representation to Mr. Brdjanin, for Mr. Brdjanin to continue to have a fair trial in this case. I know that's a large request but I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you're not going to get it, Mr. Ackerman. I'm afraid I have the responsibility for -- for managing this trial, as I have explained before, I am not prepared to take the risk of a working to a schedule which will not allow for any calamity, for any contingency that might arise. What you are saying is, and what the Prosecution has put forward, is absolutely unacceptable to me. We have to finish the case for the Prosecution by the 1st of August. If there is cross-examination, that you cannot cope with, I will reserve it for you and you will conduct it when you are dealing with your case later on when we start with the Defence. But I am not in a position -- for example, a week ago, we had absolutely no idea that were you coming forward and telling us I am tired, we are tired, we need a week off. And this is what I mean. A week ago, we were told examination-in-chief we only require five minutes more, ten minutes more, and then all of a sudden it was 35 minutes. I simply cannot go on like this. I'm afraid I have allowed you, both the Prosecution and the Defence, too much space and what has happened is that we are now in the position where I need to discipline you, both of you, according to what I consider to be absolutely necessary for this case to finish by the deadline that circumstances have put. So I understand that this may not be easy but don't put me in a position where I have to react and say we cannot go on like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you've just suggested a solution which I think is probably satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this, Mr. Ackerman, one moment, because next week I'm going to be told that Mr. Cunningham needs to go to the States and I understand that and that you will be shouldering the burden yourself for a whole week. Share the burden as you like, but please don't let me stop for one single hour between now and the 1st of August and we have to finish by the 1st of August. If you're not in a position to conduct the cross-examination, we will leave it until later but we have to finish by the 1st of August. And this is something which is at my prerogative as the Presiding Judge and I will be the one who will be taking decisions and I'm not going to budge for one single minute on this 1st August deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully understand that it's your prerogative and I'm certainly not standing here trying to tell you what to do. I was simply making a request. But you have come up with a solution that I think is satisfactory so I'm satisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there is one problem that arises out of that. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is more than one problem, Ms. Korner. I'm going to send you back offering you to withdraw it instead of me ordering that it be expunged from the records of this case. You sent us a Prosecution submission of statement of expert witness pursuant to Rule 94 bis. This is the expert on propaganda, a Croat educated in Slovenia, who starts her report by saying: "The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia commissioned the content analysis of official documents of Republika Srpska Autonomous Region of Krajina, certain municipalities and the Serbian Democratic Party." When did we commission this lady to make this report for us? That's number 1. The task of the researchers at the Faculty of Social Sciences University of Ljubljana was to analyse the content of official documents and mass media and to establish a connection between the propaganda activities and the events that took place on the ground. A special attention was given to the role played by the indicted persons, Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic in this process. Is this the purpose of an expert witness to tell us that the accused is guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I'm sorry, that's a total misreading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a total misreading. Three-fourths of the report is what Mr. Brdjanin may have said on TV. What Mr. Brdjanin is reported to have said in the newspaper. Is that an expert's report?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look at what Mr. Brdjanin said within the context of how propaganda works, that there would be no point in making a -- producing a report that didn't look at anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've got it all rote. We will not accept any expert report or report of an expert witness which deals precisely with the activities of the accused, an expert witness is here to tell us, give us his expertise on a particular matter and not to testify on the accused. That's number 1. Secondly, because we are supposed to have commissioned this content analysis, we have also selected the documents on which this report is being based.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is what the report says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They have to make a selection, Your Honour there is thousands and thousands of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who made the selection?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They made the selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who made the selection?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, they made the selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. The researchers examined the material that the ICTY made available for us. We made the material available to them. So you have got until the end of today to withdraw this document and second thing, if it is represented with the contents regarding Mr. Talic, General Talic, and Mr. Brdjanin, the Defence is going to be exempted, dispensed with any cross-examination and that gives you an indication of how much importance we are going to give it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that event, the expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is an abuse of the whole idea of being allowed to get here an expert witness, an abuse, a blatant abuse.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our submission, it is not an abuse. It is a perfectly proper aspect of an expert's report that they should look at what the defendant or the accused said. Your Honour, I'm sorry that it said the ICTY. I didn't pick that up when I reread it. If Your Honour rules that we can't call that witness, then Your Honour will rule that we can't call that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that it has not been disclosed within the 30 days that is specified, contemplated by the Rules --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason it hasn't been disclosed is because, Your Honour, we disclosed it in time had we been sitting at the end of August, because she was going to testify then. That was dealt with before Your Honour made the ruling that we were not to sit beyond the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry, I will not accept that explanation. It's absolutely --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is Your Honour saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is not an explanation --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is Your Honour saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- with regard to other expert witnesses the report was disclosed months before, months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually not, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, no? Of course not. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is Your Honour suggesting that I'm lying to Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm suggesting that there is no reason why this should not or could not have been disclosed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we got the report from the expert, I can't remember the date, but a couple of days before it was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, there is no reason why you should not have insisted for it before, because this deals with General Talic so it is a report that must have been written months and months and months ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it wasn't a report. There was a draft that was written, then there was further information that came in. Your Honour, one of the difficulties we've had throughout with experts is that we have been translating documents as we go through the trial. And so as these documents come up, they clearly become relevant. Now, Your Honour, we got this report, I don't know how many days before, we told Your Honour because it was on the original application and list, that the expert could not testify until the end of August. That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because she had her holiday booked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's correct, and if Your Honour looks at the original submission for timing that we put in, this would have been disclosed well within the 30 days. I hope Your Honour will accept that. If Your Honour does not accept it, well, then I hope Your Honour will tell me because there were certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, that is beside the point at this point in time, Ms. Korner. I think we cannot accept on record a report which starts with an affirmation which is not true. Which is false.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you cannot use language like that. It was an error on that part, but to say it is not true ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is absolutely not true. It's not an error, Ms. Korner. It's not an error. One day anyone who is studying the records of this case will come across this report which makes out of this as an ex officio expert and not as an ex parte expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can put a correction in but for Your Honour to suggest that this was done deliberately to mislead is in my submission simply an outrageous suggestion. These are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't use that language, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour is using language which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am using language which arises out of the face of the document. If anyone reads this document that person is going to conclude that this is a report by an expert appointed by the Tribunal and that is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, that was an error. I'm merely quarrelling with your language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, Ms. Korner, take it back because we are not going to accept it any way. And if it is represented in the form that it is, dealing precisely with Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic, I told you precisely from -- as from now what use we are going to put to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour has every right to reject the filing and that is an end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is not an expert witness report. That is evidence on the accused using the pretext of expertise to tell the Tribunal the accused is guilty. Please find him guilty. And we will not accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say this? Propaganda is merely Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one element. They are not saying that the accused is guilty. Propaganda goes to the counts of persecutions and genocide. They are saying within the scheme of propaganda, this is how the defendant's utterances come. It's a different matter to say, "You should find him guilty." Your Honour, that's not what the report says and not for one moment does it say that. It simply says, "We are experts in the use of propaganda, here is the model and this is what the defendant's utterances come into within that model," and it's for Your Honours to accept or reject that expert evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Expert evidence should be an evidence on a particular matter on which the Tribunal needs expertise. But the Tribunal does not need expertise to understand or to look at a particular newspaper cutting or a particular video recording or a particular transmission or the transcript of a speech. We don't need an expert. We will reach the decision ourselves when we read those transcripts and for an expert to come here and try to influence us basing herself or himself on the supposed expertise, influencing us that according to expert there is no way we could look at those documents but in an incriminating manner is an abuse of the process. An expert should not -- an expert should never involve himself or herself in deciding a matter which the Tribunal has to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is perfectly entitled to say we don't need expert evidence on this. That's a totally different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you, Ms. Korner that if we had appointed an expert on propaganda, we would certainly not have chosen a Croat or a Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is simply a suggestion said in open public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That someone who because they happen to be a Croat cannot give an unbiased opinion. Your Honour, that is simply something which in our submission ought not to be said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think everyone would feel much more comfortable if an independent, someone who has absolutely nothing to do with the whole story and who doesn't come from the region, from the area, it would have been much, much better and I can assure you we would never dream of appointing as an expert witness or as an expert someone who has come -- who comes from the region or who even on the face of it may send even though there is absolutely no shadow of -- to indicate that this is so. But the idea of throwing into the arena someone coming from the area itself to tell us whether the Serbian propaganda machine was conducive to what happened, do you think it's wise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are Slovenians, they are acknowledged experts and have published on the propaganda of the region. It is also important that whoever deals with this is able to speak the language but, Your Honour, I think we are now, with respect, wasting what is -- Your Honour has made clear is valuable time. I hear what Your Honour says. Your Honour is rejecting the report. You do not need expertise on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not saying that, Ms. Korner. I am saying I will not in the first place accept a report which on the face of it presents itself as being a report commissioned by this Tribunal when this is not so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can certainly make that absolutely clear but as it's served on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I don't think anybody will think that the Tribunal ordered this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I simply don't understand how you think that, Ms. Korner, because anyone who reads this report can only think that it has been commissioned by the ICTY. Which is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is nothing more I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither do I. Neither do I. I think we can bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that, please, first, in the light of what Your Honours do -- I take it Your Honour's ruling is that there will be no further time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course there will be no further time. Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the question that I stood to ask Your Honour was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is going to be an extension for the Rule 98 bis for sure, both of you. I mean both Prosecution and the Defence. We still have to discuss some of the details but there we are going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We would prefer, and I make this absolutely clear as I have to Your Honour, that the witnesses who are coming up are so important that we would prefer to have the extra time to call the witness rather than the extension of the Rule 98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You'll get that if Mr. Ackerman withdraws his request for more time to file the Rule 98 bis motion. If he withdraws that and restricts it to two weeks and you cut it down to seven days, then yes we might consider that. Otherwise not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my application is again, that because of the importance of these witnesses, and indeed to accommodate Mr. Ackerman's desire for further cross-examination, that we be given at the very least that week at the end of August. But Your Honour, the second thing is this: If cross-examination is adjourned until after the close of the Prosecution case, and goes into, as it were, the Defence case, then, Your Honour, how is that evidence to be treated for the purposes of Rule 98? Because there has been no cross-examination, whereas we will want to rely on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There you have a point, yes, but we are not going to beyond the 1st of August deadline. So you have to make arrangements, you yourself. I have a document here which goes back to May in which you indicated that you were already concerned that there is a great possibility that we will impose a time limit within which you have to finish your case, and the time limit has come, the 1st of August, and we not going to budge on that. I can assure you there ask no way we can budge on that, except as I said there is two weeks and one week then maybe we can contemplate that but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to carry this on because it seems to me it's a pointless argument but I would remind Your Honours that for a very long time I've been asking about this, and for a very long time I have been objecting to the weeks off that we had. And, Your Honour, it's in the interests -- I hope I've made this clear, of Your Honours coming to a just conclusion to the international community who are following this trial that witnesses of the importance who are coming up now are unable to give their evidence fully and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not my problem. You chose to leave Kotor Varos to the very end, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, because Your Honour gave me no indication that we would have this happening to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner had examination-in-chief been kept within the number of hours and number of days that you had indicated as we went along, we would have finished something like four or five months ago. Unfortunately, what we were told was going to be a one-day witness became two or sometimes three-day witness. What was a two-day witness became three- or four-day witness as we went along and I certainly cannot blame it on the Defence. I'm being very plain on this. I simply can blame it on bad management of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that leads me to the next question: How much time are you going to give me for the witness today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time do you require, Mr. Ackerman, for cross-examining this witness? I know that this is an important witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm still in the middle of preparation. It's looking to me like about a day and a half. That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you had planned to have this witness here for two days or three days, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two days. Will the -- how much time do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour has seen the list of entries that I would like to refer to. It's a question of what Your Honours -- Your Honour said you were going to impose a time limit. I would suggest it is a little unfair to say I will be given one hour and Mr. Ackerman a full day and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have a diary which we can read and you have summarised it for us by pages so I frankly don't know what you want to ask your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to draw the attention of the witness to various entries and ask him about how they were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you compare this witness with the other two that you have the rest of the week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The one, the following, is obviously an important witness from the point of view of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you limit yourself to presenting the statement of the next witness and reserving the rest of the time for cross-examination and the same with the other witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. So it's your problem. I don't know. I will give you one hour and you have to finish within one hour, today's witness. In fact, when we met in my chambers that Monday or Tuesday, you yourself said that you could easily present the diary and let Mr. Ackerman do the cross-examination without even putting any questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I could but it would be a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you said you could and if you could if I give you one hour, that's more than enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honour. There is one other matter and that is that the witness is very concerned that there are a large number of people mentioned in his diary, full name, who are still living in Banja Luka. At the moment, the pages will be brought up on the screen. That of course will mean that sometimes the names are visible to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what do you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest closed session. I don't see how it's going to work otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Same position always, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think what Ms. Korner is suggesting, I went through what I could on this, here -- I think it's wise to go into closed session. What I doubt is whether we should be closed session throughout the whole evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to me that we don't have to project the documents on the screen. We have them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The judges only have them on CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently the Registrar is saying otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we can direct the witness to avoid mentioning names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not -- the fact is that he's going -- the diary in English will go up on the screen. I mean there is no other way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it have to go on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can't we keep that from going outside the courtroom? Can't we just block that part from going outside?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Rather than go to full closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's agree on this. We will -- I don't think that we need to -- and if we need to at any particular moment then we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The alternative to not putting the page up on the screen or whatever is for me to ask the witness to read out the entry which is a complete waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you can direct the witness to the entry. He reads it without reading it aloud and then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I take it the concern is not having it on -- not with the problem with having it on the scene in the courtroom but having it broadcast outside this courtroom. And I think the audiovisual people can simply keep it within the courtroom so it's not broadcast outside and that solves the problem, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not technical enough to know whether that is possible or not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible, Your Honour. We simply not to broadcast that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I want it make sure that the technicians have grasped the whole idea.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I believe so. You have assurance of our technicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It's not a question of doubting what they will do. I want to make sure that they know precisely what's expected of them. All right. So the witness does not enjoy --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He does, yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have to bring down the curtains for a while, until he comes in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's image only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is it BT97?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, 94. No voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's check for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- there was -- this was BT94? No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is pseudonym -- good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence very shortly. Before you do so, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath. The text is contained in the document that you've just been given. Please read it outloud and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, please take your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the first time you are giving evidence before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The procedure is pretty much similar to what it is in basically all domestic jurisdictions. You will first be asked a series of questions by Ms. Korner who is appearing for the Prosecution and then she will be followed by Mr. Ackerman who is representing Mr. Brdjanin in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this case and who will cross-examine you. You asked for some protective measures, namely image distortion and a pseudonym. You will not be referred to by your name in the course of these proceedings. You are going to be referred to by a number. You are BT94. And if you look at your monitor, and the cameras focus on you, this is how others will be seeing you outside this courtroom. May I ask the cameraman to focus the camera on the witness, please. This is how others will see you and that is image distortion. Thank you. Ms. Korner

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, can you have a look, please, at a piece of paper and just identify that you're the person referred to there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that please be made P2323 under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go, please, and ask you a few questions about your background and I'd like to go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During the course of the events of 1992, and 1993, did you keep a diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. I kept a diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you just tell Their Honours how you would make the entries in the diaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: To start with, it was supposed to be a diary. I wrote about personal impressions, about everything that was going on around me, but then the diary developed into a black chronicle of my town and there were, in the end 150 people who were bringing me information that I was entering.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your diary, as Their Honours have seen, having read through the whole thing, there are quotes from Glas, and in many cases articles as well as other newspapers. How would you record those in your diary? In other words, was it a summary or would you copy word for word what was in the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, that depended on the type of the text, what kind of interview it was. Sometimes I literally transcribed everything. In fact in most of the cases if I thought that there should be a trace, that it should be recorded and remembered, that is what I entered into my diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will also see, in the diary, although we may not see it in court today, but in the diary are contained full -- what appear to be full transcripts of radio interviews. How did you record those in your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I recorded radio programmes which I thought to be interesting. I recorded news, particularly interviews with the then leading personalities, and then I would transcribe it. I would type it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you keep the tapes, the cassettes or whatever you were recording on or did you then reuse them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: For a while, I kept them, but later on, I was no longer able to do that because I had no money to buy new tapes so then after I transcribed a recording, I would then reuse the tapes for a new recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm afraid, sir, I've been given a time limit on how long I can ask you questions for, so I'm going to ask you, please, just to look at one or two entries. I'm going to ask, Your Honour, that his statements be made an exhibit now, if I'm to be given so little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. [Microphone not activated] Is there any objection on your part, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the statements --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are three statements Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's identify them and give them a number straight away. Which one do you want to start with?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we better take them in chronological order. The first is the 9th of October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second is the 24th of November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, one moment. So this will be the first one? P?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like them maybe P2324.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next one is 24 November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it would be 2324.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the last made yesterday will be .3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the last one made yesterday? Because I don't have it. I don't have the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I take it Your Honour would take it as if the witness has said every word that's in these statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can I take you just to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In light of what Ms. Korner just said, it seems to me, if the Court is going to take it that he said every word that's in the statements, then there should be some oath by him that what he said in the statements is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. I would expect Ms. Korner to put that question. I don't think she needs to be directed by the Trial Chamber on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I think you followed that. You made three statements to the investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor. Is what you said in those statements true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: It is absolutely the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection obviously because they were taken ten years or so after the events, is your -- what you said in there accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. It is accurate, and because I relied on my diary, I was not remembering, I was writing things down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to have a look, please at a couple of entries only. First of all, Thursday, the 27th of February. If somebody would like to give it to him, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can the documents be placed on the ELMO or else could the interpreters be provided with copies of the diary?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think this particular entry can go on to the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- do you have it available in the English language?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's going to come up on the screen, or we'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see on the screen is something completely different at the moment. Usher, if you have the English version -- Ms. Gustin?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have it now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You will see there at the top, sir, you were recording that on the 27th of February, 1992, there was an explosion and damage to the tomb of somebody called Pasa Sokolovic, builder of a mosque named after him, which completely destroyed the front door of the burial site and we can see the damage described. Did you yourself -- this was a report from Radio Banja Luka, but did you yourself see the damage to that mosque? Or tomb, I should say? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And throughout your diary, in 1992, you record attacks on mosques or some attacks on mosques. When you recorded that, did you go and have a look at the damage yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: No. I did not go every time, but I had people who did that, and who enjoyed my complete confidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But on this one you did see yourself, did you, this damage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you, please, to move on in your diary to the 29th of February. And if we -- I'd like you to find the part where you were quoting an item of news from the radio station relating to the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And it was putting out something about the referendum that was to be held. Serbs who participate in the referendum will run afoul of their people. The troops the souls of dead heroes and so on. And then, the Serbian Democratic Party put out its own release. If you go to the next part, the next page. Right. And we see: "Do not participate in the referendum, brother and sister Serbs, it's an Islamic state, a knife at the throat of Serbian children, Serbian mothers," and so on and so forth. Throughout your diary, you record this type of what I'm going to call propaganda, and as we see throughout the time, it got worse and worse. From what you saw, what effect was this type of proclamation or things being said on media, what effect was that having on the Serbs in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, a bad influence, not just on the citizens [as interpreted], on the urban part, but particularly on the rural part. It had a catastrophic influence. They were convinced they were under threat, and every word that was uttered through the media represented a law to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you listen to radio programmes where people rang in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember any particular type of radio programme where it could be seen what effect this type of propaganda was having?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, if you have enough patience, I can, for instance, mention one, just one programme, of the type, and that was evening talk show hosted by Milinko Stojicic, a journalist. It was a live programme. People phoned in and made their comments. Now, I can't tell you exactly the day when it was on, but you can find it in the diary. There was a threat of the NATO to bomb part of the -- of Republika Srpska because of all that was happening there, and the programme was organised in relation to that. So listeners began to call in and, for instance, I remember a man and his name I noted down because he introduced himself quite openly, and then -- he was from Sanski Most, and he said, "Just let them try. In Sanski Most, we have 5.000 Muslims there. If they throw their bombs, we know what we will do with our Muslims and you can do with yours whatever you think you should do with them." The host, the anchor never tried to bring the tension down, to placate these people and the programme just went on. The next day, I learned that it was exactly at the time when this programme was aired a zolja had been fired at the mosque in Potok, and at the time when this programme was on air, on Rudarska Street, Nermin Djumisic, now I can't swear to his name, but again I have his name there, and I think his -- was stabbed with knives in his home and an open Koran was put over his head. So this is one of the examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour there is a translation error that's important. Page 28, line 9, the answer reads, "Well, a bad influence, not just on the citizens." I'm told that what he said was: "Not that much on the citizens, on the urban part." In other words, instead of "not just," it should say, "not that much."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear what Mr. Ackerman said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree with what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I said, and I think you quoted me correctly, that it didn't have all that much influence on town dwellers, on townsmen, as on rural part of the population, on rural dwellers and later on it escalated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you now, please, have your diary for July, please? The 15th. 15th of July I want you to look at first, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I must say I can't really find my way about this, can somebody help me. Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, when we, according to you, should not be transmitting, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because otherwise, I would not be in a position myself to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, did you -- sorry -- did you have a conversation with the then-editor of Glas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I did, yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: No, Miro Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was he the editor of Glas at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at that stage, and Their Honours will be familiar with it, there was a massive row, I think, going on between the Glas and the Crisis Staff in Banja Luka or the War Presidency as it then became known. Is that correct? Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: It is, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all right. Now, look, here you speak to him and you tell him that you would like to encourage him in his fight against the powerful triumvirate whom he, to a large extent, helped in becoming almost untouchable in this area. Can you just tell us who you meant by the powerful triumvirate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Why, those were Brdjanin, Kupresanin, Vukic. A triumvirate? Well, actually it was a quartet because there was the Mayor Radic there too. They were people who destroyed our town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You later described them in your diary as the four horsemen of the apocalypse. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: For centuries, Banja Luka promoted coexistence. It was a multi-religious, multi-cultural, multi-ethnic centre. After the earthquake in Banja Luka in 1969, because of the damage done to the Catholic church, the Serb Orthodox Church invited the Catholics, that is Croats, to have their religious services in its church, because there indeed was cohabitation there, and when those four emerged, and after they took over the power, flying on the wings of the Serb defence forces, life became unbearable, chaos set in, and after all, ladies and gentlemen, you all know what Banja Luka turned into at the time, the biggest concentration camp in the world. And another thing, if I may add, I know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from my own experience, that over 300 young men of Muslim and Croat ethnicity, who fortunately had left Banja Luka with the IDs of their Serb friends, that is those boys gave them their ID cards and we put in photographs and forged stamps to enable them to get out through the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If you go to the next page, please, of -- it's the next page in our translation. And can we not have this go out, please? Because that does give some names. I don't know, is it going out or not? All right. 48328. And you will see there that you spoke with some of the detainees who were brought from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see references to the camps throughout your diary. Was the existence of these camps known to the people in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Sure, of course, of course they knew about it. We knew about those camps. People talked about it. You can't hide anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your experience of life in Banja Luka in this period, is it conceivable that those in authority, any one of the four horsemen did not know of the existence of the camps in Omarska and Keraterm and Manjaca and the like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Out of the question, out of the question, absolutely. They all knew about them and after all, they visited that camp, for instance Mr. Brdjanin went to Omarska, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I think I had it recorded. I think I have an audio tape, which I managed to obtain. And it contains a statement of a lady who testified, but was a detainee and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The audiotape was not furnished to the Defence. In addition, my understanding is that the Prosecution don't even know the name of this person who allegedly made such a statement on tape. It doesn't -- this doesn't appear anywhere in the diary of this witness, and I therefore object to the whole matter being brought up at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's an audiotape with an unnamed -- there is a first name given, an unnamed woman talking about her experiences in Omarska. That's what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But has it been disclosed to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, because we don't rely on it and it doesn't take this case any further. But he's giving his reason as opposed to whether it's true or not, for why he believes Mr. Brdjanin went to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can leave it at that, anyway. I don't think there should be any further questions on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. You didn't bring this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are not going to make use of it? Right. Okay, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you describe here the man who explained how he'd come to Sanski -- to Manjaca and the conditions that were in that camp. Were the conditions, and let's just concentrate on Manjaca for a moment, known to people in Banja Luka generally? If we move to the next page, 329? And that can go out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. People knew that. You know how it is. For instance, specifically, I was told about the conditions in the Manjaca camp by a man who was a guard there. He told me about the things that went on there and how terrible they were and so on and so forth. I can give you his name. He's called Momir Dragic. Of course people knew what went on there. I had a friend who was arrested, he was a Catholic, so they took him in on Christmas so that he would spend Christmas there, and he even drew what that camp, Manjaca, looked like, and wrote a few words about it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, please, to the 1st of August, please. This is another topic I just want to touch on through your diary. You say there on the 31st of July: "Today, six busloads of people wishing to leave Banja Luka set out for Croatia in the reorganisation of the resettlement --" I'm sorry, "in the organisation of the resettlement agency and the Red Cross." Now, during this period in 1992, was this an unusual number of buses to be leaving or was it a regular occurrence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: That was already in August, 1992. In August, 1992, it was already happening. Well, I won't say a regular occurrence, but I'd say it was quite a frequent occurrence. Perka Bandic in Mejdan and many others organised the transport. These six buses -- well, that was perhaps a major thing that day, but every day there would be two or three leaving. This was perhaps the first sizeable transport and perhaps that is why I put it in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've mentioned Perka Bandic. What was her role in all of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: She headed this intermediary agency for the resettlement of persons. You had to go through her, through her and some other agencies which I didn't mention here. Perhaps I don't even know them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about -- there were every day two or three buses leaving. Would you agree with a suggestion that there was something like one a week at most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: More than that, more than that. Many more. Once a week? No. We saw them day in, day out. (Redacted) (Redacted) I saw huge crowds next to the workers' centre where that was happening. There would always be a throng of people, a multitude of people waiting there, queueing to get out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like, please, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Redacted?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And line eight redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Madam Registrar, line 7 and the first part of line 8. In other words, the beginning of the sentence in line 7 and where you have a comma before the words, "And whenever." Those need to be deleted, or redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was making all these people leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: It's simple. They simply could not survive there any longer because they had been sacked from their jobs because they had not responded to the call-up. They simply refused to kill, and so they were fired. They were given notice in their companies. People had nothing to eat, whilst they still had some they sold whatever they had at home, but after that, they shall -- there was simply no way to eke out a living any way. So those people could not survive there. There simply were no means of livelihood or of existence in the town for them any longer, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could we move now to another aspect of life in Banja Luka? Tuesday, the 4th of August, please. Now, on that page, sir, you describe how you were in front of the Mejdan police station and you saw the red van with registration plates and you give those, as well as the group of seasoned hunters, you say, in camouflage uniform armed to the teeth. These rascals drive around in the wretched van and never bother shutting the door whenever they spot a large concentration of people and they search, you go on to say they search people and so on and so forth. Did you -- you saw the red van there. Did you yourself know about this particular red van before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Of course I did, of course. I had really focused on investigating, of finding out who was it in that van. And in time, I learned the names of all of them. It was, I think, one of the most horrendous things that went on in Banja Luka. At night, they would circle around the town or perhaps of evening, of late afternoon, they would round up a group of people and put them in the van, and in the middle of the van there was a noose and they would put the noose around the person's neck and the person -- and then they would drive, while the man had to crouch on the floor, and whenever the driver would turn a corner or something, that person of course would start falling down and the noose would tighten around that person's neck. I mean, it was a -- heaven forbid. At a funeral, if I may add, of a woman, they turned up in the middle of the burial ceremony and they went to the sheet, to the cover in which the -- the shroud in which a Muslim is wrapped, and when people started to weep, they began to beat them, and that was the role of the red van, and this is another answer to a question about why people were leaving Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you then to move in your diary to the 5th of August, and you recorded there the length of time that you had been writing this diary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I can't really find it. It's a long time since I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's about two pages after the beginning of the entry for that day. It's a paragraph that begins: "It has been 218 days since I started following developments in this misfortunate city."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Just -- just a moment, please. Be patient with me. I've reached the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was directed to the 15th of August by the translation rather than the 5th. That's why he's confused. If he goes to the 5th of August, he'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you -- usher, it's marked, if you could turn it up the 5th of August, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: The 5th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: My apologies. I understood you were talking about the 15th. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All I want to ask you about that is everybody can read what you said. Are those the reasons that you felt at the time that it was necessary to record, and which you still feel today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. Of course these are the reasons. Quite simply I could see what was happening and I felt the impulse to write it down so that it can stay behind, so that it can be remembered, so that it is not forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just two other aspects, please, then. Could you move now -- just forgive me one moment -- to the 11th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You refer there to: "In Celinac Muslims are allowed to move around for not more than four hours a day and people in mixed marriages are also in disfavour. A Serbian woman married to a Muslim will be fired." And then you deal with Brdjanin. How did you hear about these laws that prevented various Muslims from moving around Celinac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, some people from Banja Luka worked there. For instance, I had friends who worked there. For instance, a nurse whom I knew worked there. And in the diary you can find her name, and you know it. I'd rather not mention her because she has stayed behind. She was, for instance, one of those who told me about these things. And besides, it was no secret. Come, Mr. Brdjanin never tried to conceal his feelings. He was always quite open-minded. He was the happiest when he appeared on the radio, and when he could talk. True, he always mentioned honest Muslims and honest Croats, and those were those who found excuses even for things such as, say, the red van. They were honest. And if somebody said that this was madness, that this was not all right, well that person was not honest and that person had to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to break here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I still have ten minutes left of the hour Your Honour allotted me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need to break here and we will continue after the break. Can we shorten the break to 20 minutes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's okay with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That would give Ms. Korner an extra ten minutes. You will have 20 minutes in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, throughout your diary, as we've all seen, you record explosions, shooting, and give accounts of people who to your knowledge were beaten. I want to ask you about one occasion when you actually saw the results of one of these beatings by the authorities. Could you could have your diary, please, for the 27th of August, 1992? And I'd prefer -- yes, thank you, no, this should not go out, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Technicians, please take note of that. Madam Registrar, check that, because I don't know how to check it. All right. Okay. What I mean to say is I don't have the means to check it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 27th of August, did you actually not only take a statement from someone who was beaten up by the police but also photographs of his injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. I did. Except that I'd like to make a slight correction, I'm sorry, this is not the only person that I'd seen who had been beaten up. There were many people who had been beaten up but I was in a situation to bring a doctor to him. The person was spitting blood and I had to somehow look after him. I brought a friend who was a doctor, and who came to examine him, and to administer some help, and I also got another friend of mine who was a journalist, a colleague of mine, in fact he's a photojournalist, he worked for many newspapers and he photographed him and these are the photographs that I attached to my diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, please, and identify the photographs that you took -- or that were taken in your presence. And I think they can go on to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. These are the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think there are some other ones. If you turn over --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: There are more, there are more photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... other side, please, usher.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes, these are the photographs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that please be made Exhibit 2325? Your Honours, I think in fact what we better do is produce colour photocopies and makes those the exhibits because this has to go back to the evidence unit, the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that agreeable with you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I now want to move, please, in your diary to the 29th of August, please. The first page is 4418 and then 4419. I think there you were recording or recording in your diary a discussion with Dr. Milan Subotic and as you describe on the previous page the unavoidable Brdjanin, and you record there that Brdjanin stated in respect -- this is after the camps obviously had been discovered -- sorry, can we get 54419 up? Thank you. A bit further up. Thank you. Brdjanin saying: "When I first came to Banja Luka as a child, I really thought that this was a Muslim city, as all the leading positions were occupied by Muslims. If Hitler, Stalin and Churchill could have working camps, why could not we? We are in a war, after all."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I can't find where we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look at the screen, you'll see it up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I can't find it in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's L0054419 is the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 28 August, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Throughout your diary you record a lot of Brdjanin's sayings. How did that strike you at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, that was a habitual way in which this was done. It's nothing special, really. I mean the way that Brdjanin addressed himself to the wide audience through the mass media, to be honest, one thing that has to be said for him is that he was the bravest one because for the most part his statements and I think all of them, all of the announcements he -- he was sober when he said that, while Vukic, for instance, when he made his public announcements, he was mostly drunk, and they provoked panic among the people. But for -- as for Brdjanin, he thought he was a God's gift to the masses. He decided on life and death. He thought that was his right. I'm not saying here that he really wanted bad things to happen to Croats and Muslims. I don't want to say that. But the way he addressed himself, the way he spoke, in his public announcements, in the mass media, the way he spoke, he caused panic among the people. That is what he did. That's a fact. And this case in question is nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. All right. Can we move into September, please? First of all, the 2nd of September. And if we just move up the page there, we'll see -- don't worry, sir, you needn't turn it up because you were recording, as you stated, yet more people leaving Banja Luka. And you end up by saying: "Only the most persistent, like me, are staying and those who cannot afford the journey." Now, can we look, please, at your recording of an eyewitness apparently to a massacre? First of all, on the 4th of September, at -- this is 54916. You -- yes, you record the radio reporting that soldiers had killed about 250 Muslims, somewhere around Travnik, while the Trnopolje camp that was being relocated, and you'd heard that also, as it were, second or thirdhand, as we can see. But then if we move, please, to the 7th of September --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you there had a conversation with a Lieutenant Peulic, son of the commander of the same name, Bosko Peulic, I think it is, who described to you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the massacre as it's come to be called that took place on Mount Vlasic. And if we move, please, to the next page --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: May I just say something very briefly? This was a recording, a friend of mine in the cafe bar called Formula recorded the drunken Davor Peulic who was speaking about this. And later on I met a Serb soldier who in fact even introduced me into the hospital where I saw a great deal of time [as interpreted], and this soldier was -- had been there and had seen all of those corpses at the location, and he had told me that this had been carried out by the Prijedor police, not the army. That was his opinion. That's what he told me, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you move now to the 17th of September? I want it look at something that was said by one of the top Serbian leaders, Bosnian Serb leaders. I think you were recording, if we look at 47328, a programme called Open Screen, and the subject was genocide. The guests were Velibor Ostojic, Mr. Petrovic, Davidovic and Deretic. Could you find the part where you're recording what Mr. Ostojic had to say after there had been a discussion of the Vatican by Mr. Petrovic? And then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Ostojic said this: "To my mind, the Muslims are not an ethnic group but yet another socialist realist creation." And if we go on over the page, although it's not quite the point, he said, "There were no prisons, let alone concentration camps, there was only a prison in Manjaca. All the others were collection centres." Now, throughout this period, you record the visit of the top leadership, the Bosnian Serb leadership, as well as internationals. Did you get the -- from hearing what they said on radio programmes, that there was any difference in the attitude taken to non-Serbs by the Banja Luka leadership, Brdjanin and the like, and those at the top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, in the essence, no. For instance, Biljana Plavsic was one of the most extremist ones, if I may say so. As far as Karadzic is concerned, we all know what he was like. But they perhaps sometimes spoke in some softened terms and Mr. Brdjanin said, "we Krajina people," we know, and I'm speaking that I believe is supported by the majority of the Serb people. Our ones, so to speak, the local ones, Brdjanin, Vukic, Kupresanin and Radic, for instance, although Radic not to such an extent, they went one step ahead. That was a fact. Even occasionally Karadzic, the way he was, seemed to be a lamb, a dove, compared to our ones, compared to our leaders, our party leaders. I don't know what to call them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I'm sorry, I've reached the end of my allotted time limits so I can't ask you any further questions but thank you very much, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman. You are an educated person so I will restrict myself to what is essentially necessary. Mr. Ackerman here is doing his duty and he has an obligation to look after the rights of his client to the best of his ability. He's also got a right on behalf of his client to cross-examine you which means that you have an obligation to answer all the questions that are put to you in accordance with the oath that you took at the beginning of your testimony. You have no right to, in other words, make a distinction between questions coming from the Prosecution and questions coming from the Defence. Mr. Ackerman, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have, what seems like I have, spent a significant part of my life reading your diary. It is quite a long piece of work, as you know. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: I'm so sorry if I have tired you out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What gave you the idea in the first place to create this diary? What was the impetus that made you want to do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: You know, I think I did say a few words about this but I will repeat. We lived in a town where, for instance, nobody knew, I think half of my friends did not know what my ethnicity was, and I didn't know what their ethnicity was. It was not an important factor. We lived a normal life, and then some horrible things started to happen. Because of the -- in the -- on behalf of a nation, ethnicity, people lost their jobs, lost their flats, were expelled from their apartments, were beaten up. When I saw that, when I saw all that, where all this was leading to, I wanted to record it, for a trace to remain from all that. That was what made me do this. And apart from that, if I hadn't done that, I would have gone mad. In this way, I was releasing some tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, you -- from what we have before us here, you started this process in January of 1992, well before a lot of these things you just described had happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you actually work on this diary every day? I mean was it something you did every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Occasionally, I would even write for six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it the case, then, that you didn't have any employment, that were you simply free to spend as much time as you wanted to or needed to to work on this diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT94
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's what it meant, (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right, Ms. Korner. I was about to say that. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This should be redacted and I'd ask Mr. Ackerman to be more careful please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I'll be more careful. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I was prepared to ask the next question on what I believe to be a 24 February 1992 section of the diary and I was sitting here looking through the 24 February 1992 section of the diary and the translation I have is from some other date obviously because the material contained in there is not in the 24 February 1992 version of the diary.
